judge: Claude Code subagent, Claude Opus 5.5, fresh

items.label: A
items.critique: Flat, offhand gossip about politics and necromancers; short exclamations with no punchline structure, typical of Westwood's ambient lines.

items.label: B
items.critique: Missing final period, plain statement of the quest hook (a stolen scepter), a sardonic aside about the last one sent; unpolished in Westwood's way.

items.label: C
items.critique: Repetitive phrasing ('If you're smart you'll leave [Place], too'), defeatist bluntness ('Let them take it, I say'); plot-tied and unjokey.

items.label: D
items.critique: The brush-off opener is plausible, but the merchants-on-the-east-road lament and 'Imps will take anything that shines' read as composed regional flavour.

items.label: E
items.critique: Typo ('off you back'), the same spider/mayor content repeated by two speakers, plain worry; this redundancy and roughness is Westwood's.

items.label: F
items.critique: Every line is a crafted quip ('Poor man looks worse than they do!'); 'hasn't slept a wink' recurs across several texts in the packet.

items.label: G
items.critique: Cow, pitchfork-under-the-bed rumour, turnip brush-off: a neat one-joke-per-line set built on the same phrases seen in F, I and J.

items.label: H
items.critique: Lowercase 'ogres', the self-own 'Maybe we shouldn't have built so close to the ogre village', 'Well good luck to ya' without a comma: dry Westwood humour.

items.label: I
items.critique: Busy brush-off, foreboding bog line and pitchfork rumour follow the same three-slot recipe as G and J.

items.label: J
items.critique: Hero-worship anecdote, 'haven't slept a wink', 'bread in the oven' brush-off; the praise/dread/busy formula is the new texts' signature.

tells: The new sets follow a fixed recipe of three slots (a comic brush-off like 'I've got bread in the oven', a dread line, a gossip line about a named person), and stock phrases recur across sets: 'hasn't slept a wink', 'pitchfork under his bed'.
Each new line is a finished joke with a punchline; Westwood's ambient lines are flatter, often a plain statement of the plot or a worry, sometimes redundant between speakers.
Westwood's lines carry small errors (missing periods, 'you back', lowercase 'ogres', missing commas); the new ones are clean.
Westwood ties townsfolk to the chapter's actual events (a stolen scepter, spiders in the mayor's house, the necromancers); the new ones lean on generic regional colour (roads, bogs, imps, weather).
